entries.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
entries.summary: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers
entries.content:
Fenghui Zhang

Distinguished Engineer, Google Cloud

Weiren Yu

Senior Product Manager, Google Cloud

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle.

We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync.

Across this shared model-state layer, TPU Sync integrates directly into existing infrastructure stacks across PyTorch (via TorchTPU) and JAX — serving as the TPU KV cache connector for vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d disaggregated serving, while providing low-level transfer primitives for Pathways and multi-controller JAX (McJAX) RL pipelines.

Understanding TPU Sync: The kitchen analogy

To understand TPU Sync’s impact, imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen. Think of the TPU as an incredibly fast executive chef working on a tiny countertop (the chip's HBM). When preparing a massive feast, the chef needs lots of ingredients (the KV cache), which quickly clutter the counter.

  • The standard kitchen (without TPU Sync): When the small counter fills up, the chef has to toss out prepped ingredients and chop them again from scratch the next time an order needs them — stalling the kitchen on repetitive prep work (prefill recomputation).

  • The upgraded kitchen (with TPU Sync): TPU Sync adds a spacious side pantry (pinned host RAM), a shared walk-in cold storage room accessible to every station in the kitchen (shared cluster storage), and a coordinated team of runners. The runners slide full prep trays directly between the counter, the pantry, and peer stations without repacking them (direct DMA in native TPU layout).

Crucially, the runners swap trays in and out while the chef keeps cooking (asynchronous, non-blocking transfers).

Key use cases for TPU Sync

TPU Sync improves system throughput and latency in workloads requiring deep context, high concurrency, multi-turn reasoning and RL rollouts:

  • Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats: When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage).

  • Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation.

  • Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead.

  • Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates.

Breaking through the memory wall with TPU Sync

At its core, TPU Sync establishes a high-performance data transfer path between TPU HBM and host RAM, as well as across TPU hosts via the DCN. It achieves this through four key architectural advantages:

  • Layout-preserving direct DMA with in-place buffer aliasing: TPU Sync accesses the underlying JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place and moves slices directly between TPU HBM and page-locked (

    DmaMap
    -registered) host memory in a single hardware DMA. By keeping tensors in their native TPU physical tile layout across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and the wire, data lands ready for immediate Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) execution with no Python serialization, no layout conversion, and no user-space bounce buffers.

  • Compute-overlapped transfers: Rather than taking an exclusive lock or making an on-device copy of static KV cache and weight buffers, TPU Sync creates raw PJRT buffer aliases (

    PJRT_RawBuffer
    ) without holding PJRT usage locks so block-level transfers can run concurrently with active in-place computation, with built-in DMA pacing to keep large transfers from delaying kernel launches.

  • No XLA compilation in the data path: Because TPU Sync executes transfers and tile-aware strided resharding in native C++ outside the XLA graph, moving KV blocks or resharding weights across different trainer and sampler topologies does not trigger runtime compilation — keeping the data path fast and framework-agnostic.

  • High-bandwidth PCIe DMA and DCN streaming: Using the 

    raw_transfer
    library’s direct PJRT raw-buffer DMA pipeline, TPU Sync reaches up to 223 GB/s of aggregate D2H and H2D throughput per Ironwood (TPU v7x) host out of the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 hardware ceiling, and streams across the DCN at up to ~192 Gbps on a single 200 Gbps NIC (or ~350 Gbps across dual 200 Gbps NICs with NUMA-aware multi-NIC striping).

TPU Sync exposes a low-level data transfer API, making it easier for developers to integrate high-speed TPU data transfer into higher-level frameworks.

Higher-level architecture

Built on top of its core transport and resharding primitives, TPU Sync provides a modular orchestration stack for distributed cache management:

  • Global KV store: A global registry that maps prompt prefix hashes to physical cache blocks, handles dynamic lookups, and coordinates LRU eviction and tier demotion.

  • TPU Sync controller: The orchestration layer that generates transfer plans, coordinates data movement across nodes, and handles lease management and recovery.

  • KV cache manager: The local execution engine that tracks block states, manages HBM, host DRAM (including 

    /dev/shm
    warm-boot persistence) alongside experimental POSIX storage backends, and executes asynchronous DMA transfers.

Figure 1. TPU Sync operates as the model-state layer on TPU, unifying TPU HBM (Tier 1), pinned host DRAM (Tier 2), shared storage (Tier 3), and multi-host DCN under a single layout-preserving DMA data plane.

Solving disaggregated serving and prefix caching

Let us take a closer look at how TPU Sync helps with some of the use cases we listed in the earlier section. By treating host pinned memory as a substantial, high-speed Tier 2 cache, TPU Sync reduces the fragmentation and memory limits of standard HBM setups.

Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregated serving

In state-of-the-art serving topologies, prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases are isolated on separate node pools. To prevent latency bubbles, TPU Sync bridges this gap with a highly optimized, three-step pipeline:

  • Direct-DMA offloading: Once a prefill node processes an initial prompt, TPU Sync immediately moves the resulting KV blocks into pinned host RAM via its asynchronous D2H DMA path.

  • Host-to-host streaming: The TPU Sync controller then orchestrates a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) transfer, streaming the context directly to the assigned decode node.

  • Overlapped ingestion: As blocks arrive in the decode node's host RAM, TPU Sync triggers an asynchronous H2D transfer directly into TPU HBM. This happens concurrently with active decoding computation, substantially minimizing TTFT.

Host-powered prefix caching

For highly concurrent systems sharing large system prompts or running multi-turn agentic loops, TPU HBM is not large enough to hold multiple active cache blocks. TPU Sync extends the prefix cache out of HBM (Tier 1) into substantial, distributed host RAM pools (Tier 2). Because TPU Sync transfers are asynchronous, it overlaps the PCIe DMA loading of the next required prefix from host RAM with the compute of the current request — minimizing TPU idle time between requests.

For workloads that exceed even host DRAM capacity, TPU Sync also includes an experimental POSIX storage backend (Tier 3+) that asynchronously spills older KV blocks to local SSDs or shared Google Cloud Managed Lustre storage — pairing with llm-d prefix-affinity routing on GKE so replicas can recall cached prefixes across tiers without recomputing prompts.

Sample performance results

P/D disaggregated inference result highlights:

  • Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut: For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms.

  • Substantial TTFT reduction: Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency.

  • Substantial high-traffic scalability: During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution.

Prefix caching result highlights:

  • Expands KV cache capacity beyond HBM: When heavyweight MoE model weights consume most of device HBM, on-chip memory can hold only a few long-context prefixes. Offloading into pinned host DRAM expands effective cache capacity by an order of magnitude.

  • Sustains high cache-hit rates under concurrency: Pooling distributed host RAM keeps shared system prompts and multi-turn agent contexts warm across thousands of concurrent sessions instead of thrashing HBM.

  • Significantly reduces prefill recompute: Directly bypasses heavy compute layers for repeated instruction blocks and system prompts, reducing average TTFT by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads while delivering over 50% higher throughput and a 30% reduction in P99 inter-token latency (ITL).

Please see the note1 below on the testing configuration.

Ecosystem adoption and partnerships

TPU Sync serves as the open, composable memory substrate across our PyTorch-on-TPU and Kubernetes serving ecosystem, built in close collaboration with key open-source maintainers and infrastructure partners:

  • Inferact (vLLM-TorchTPU): Co-engineered with Inferact, maintainers of vLLM-TorchTPU, TPU Sync is integrated directly via vLLM's native KVConnector interface. It powers Direct-DMA host DRAM offloading and multi-host P/D disaggregation across frontier open-source models.

  • RadixArk (SGLang-TorchTPU): In partnership with RadixArk, maintainers of SGLang-TorchTPU, TPU Sync serves as both the high-speed P/D disaggregation transfer backend and the native I/O backend for SGLang’s hierarchical cache.

  • llm-d 1.0 integration: llm-d 1.0 pairs with TPU Sync on GKE to deliver global prefix-cache-affinity routing, per-rank decode session pinning, and experimental two-stage capacity spill to Google Cloud Managed Lustre.

  • Validated by frontier AI labs and enterprises: Frontier AI organizations are already adopting our PyTorch-on-TPU serving stack and evaluating TPU Sync multi-tier architectures for production deployments — including Meta, alongside major enterprises like Wayfair, and multi-silicon partners.

Get started

TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch (

tpu-sync-torch
) and JAX (
tpu-sync-jax
), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides.

We are committed to working with the open-source community to advance the model-state layer on TPU — supporting new frontier architectures, expanded storage tiering, and longer-horizon agentic and RL workloads. For more up-to-date performance results, please see our ongoing efforts on public benchmarks (InferenceX).

1. Performance results are based on internal testing conducted in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1 topology), configured with PCIe Gen5 (x16) per TPU chip and one or two 200 Gbps NICs enabled per host, running tpu-inference v0.24.0 (using JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1). Metrics presented represent average and median performance improvements observed under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual real-world performance, cache hit rates, and latency reductions will vary based on system configuration, network bandwidth, concurrent traffic, and specific user workload patterns.

entries.content:
Kavitha Gowda

Product Manager, Google Cloud

Wenzhe Li

Engineering Manager, Google Cloud, Cloud AI

Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning.

Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale.

Beyond one workload, one nodepool

Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning.

To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency.

Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams:

  • Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted.

  • Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment.

  • Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable.

  • Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes.

  • Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling.

Dynamic slicing architecture

GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube.

Dynamic super-slicing

GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency.

Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice.

How a 4x4x16 super slice (comprising 64 Ironwood VMs and 256 total chips) is formed using four Ironwood cubes (also provisioned as GKE nodepools). At runtime, the slice is created dynamically by stitching together the TPU network across all TPU chips in these four cubes.

Dynamic sub-slicing

Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy.

When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool.

How GKE sub-slicing dynamically partitions a 16-host TPU cube into smaller, independent slices (e.g., 2x2x4 with 16 chips down to 2x2x2) for optimal utilization of TPU resources.

Customer use cases

You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments.

Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE

GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation.

Getting started

Pre-provision nodepools

To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand.

Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover.

This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes.

Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing

After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations.

Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples.

Repair

When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies:

  • Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes.

  • Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions.

Next steps

Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for  TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For  working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation.

entries.content:
Amin Vahdat

Chief Technologist & SVP, AI & Infrastructure, Google

Editor’s note: This blog was originally published on News from Google.

We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more.

At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. 

Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year.

Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max.

While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads.

The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements, our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. 

Building the computer around the chip

Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system.

Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases.

When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer, so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years.

Specializing for secure, high-context AI

Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips:

  • TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used.

  • TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half.

Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale.

TPU 8tx

TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data.

Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with custom AMD CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty.

Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters.

Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution.

TPU 8i Max

Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall.

When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package.

TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt.

The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density.

While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack.

Opening up TPUs to every developer

When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code.

Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware.

This investment comes together today across these key areas:

  • Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU, so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs.

  • Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks: In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further.

  • Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our accelerators more power-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends idle agent sessions and shifts working memory off the chip in milliseconds, cutting operational infrastructure costs.

  • Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer (TPU Sync): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync, the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%.

  • Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils, you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding.

  • Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs.

Co-designing with a decade of experience

Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side.

Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator. 

Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT.

entries.content:
Shaurya Gupta

Software Engineer, Google

Monica Song

Product Manager, Google

Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways (Pathways on Cloud) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer.

Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations.

With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. We are also pleased to announce a Preview integration with Cluster Director to extend Cloud Pathways to Slurm clusters, supporting unified multi-slice JAX execution, elastic training, and interactive notebooks.

What is Cloud Pathways?

As AI workloads scale across thousands of accelerators, spanning multi-slice pre-training, disaggregated inference, and multi-program reinforcement learning (RL) loops, traditional multi-controller setups become harder to program and manage. In default multi-controller JAX, every TPU host runs its own separate Python interpreter with only a localized view of its connected devices and executes the same SPMD program in lockstep, making heterogeneous MPMD workflows and cross-slice resource management complex and brittle.

Cloud Pathways replaces multi-controller management with a unified single-controller architecture built on the open-source Interim Framework Runtime (IFRT). By setting 

JAX_PLATFORMS=proxy
with 
pathwaysutils
, a single JAX client process views and orchestrates multiple large TPU slices, spanning thousands of TPU chips as if they were all connected locally.

Learn more about Pathways in our latest deep-dive blog here.

Core architectural innovations

Cloud Pathways has the following features:

  • Single-controller orchestration: In Cloud Pathways, a single controller manages graph evaluation, persistent Cloud Storage compilation caching, and asynchronous XLA HLO dispatch across TPU slices.

  • Colocated Python sidecars: Client-side colocated Python sidecar containers (with shared-memory support) let you run compute-intensive Python logic such as distributed data loading and checkpointing directly on TPU hosts.

  • Resilient and elastic training: Cloud Pathways decouples job survival from individual slice interruptions with elastic training (

    pathwaysutils
    ) using host-memory snapshots to dynamically reshard training down to N-1 slices during hardware failures without crashing the client.

  • Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode, or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service.

Proven enterprise impact and customer momentum

Frontier AI labs, quantitative research firms, and global consumer platforms have adopted Cloud Pathways to run mission-critical production workloads on GKE, including:

  • Hyperscale multi-host inference: One of the world's largest consumer technology companies runs production batch and reinforcement learning (RL) inference on Cloud Pathways across tens of thousands of TPU v5p, Trillium (v6e), and Ironwood (TPU7x) chips, consuming over 100 million chip-hours per quarter, and co-designed elasticity primitives with Google to expand into pre-training.

  • Elastic pre-training and multi-host RL for scientific foundation models: Google Cloud customer ZenteiQ uses Cloud Pathways on GKE with Cluster Toolkit (

    gcluster
    ), colocated Python sidecars, and host snapshotting to scale elastic pre-training (
    MaxText
    ) and single-controller reinforcement learning (
    MaxText
    + 
    Tunix
    ) across multi-slice Trillium (
    v6e
    ) clusters for its scientific foundation models.

"Running multi-day pre-training and post-training jobs on high-cost accelerators requires reliable continuity through both unexpected hardware faults and planned maintenance windows. By running Cloud TPUs and MaxText with Cloud Pathways on the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer stack, ZenteiQ relies on a proven controller that monitors our TPU topology and dynamically re-meshes and resizes the workload whenever a chip or slice goes offline. Combining Pathways with host snapshotting in production pushes recovery time down to a minimum when disruptions occur, keeping our available TPU capacity fully utilized with very little stall time. Our ML engineers no longer have to spend their hours watching job health or managing manual restarts, and can stay focused on their research workloads." - Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, ZenteiQ

Getting started with Cloud Pathways

Cloud Pathways is generally available today in all Google Cloud regions supporting Cloud TPU v5e, TPU v5p, Trillium (TPU v6e), and Ironwood (TPU 7x) on GKE, with versioned container images (

us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways
) supporting JAX 
0.10.1+
. Cloud Pathways is also available in Preview on Slurm TPU clusters in Cluster Director.

To start building with Cloud Pathways:

  • Read the overview: Explore the Introduction to Pathways on Cloud in the AI Hypercomputer documentation.

  • Deploy your cluster:

  • GKE: Follow the step-by-step guide to Create a GKE cluster with Pathways using Cluster Toolkit (

    gcluster
    ) or the 
    gcloud
    CLI.

  • Slurm: Deploy Pathways via Cluster Director using the step-by-step guide.

  • Run your workloads: Dive into our production guides for Batch workloads, Interactive notebook mode, Resilient & elastic training, Multihost inference, Porting JAX workloads, and Troubleshooting.

Nov 2 - Nov 6

Join Nicola Cardace on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to safeguard enterprise AI workloads using Model Armor. Discover practical patterns for implementing active model defense across your LLM endpoints.

    Get the most out of A5X instances with Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer. Bringing together compute, storage, networking, and software co-designed as a single system. 

    Read more

Oct 26 - Oct 30

  • Simplify PostgreSQL Monitoring with the New AlloyDB Omni Web UI

    The newly released AlloyDB Omni Web UI delivers a centralized, graphical dashboard that simplifies the management of self-managed PostgreSQL workloads across hybrid, multi-cloud, and air-gapped environments. This browser-based console provides database administrators with deep, real-time insights into cluster health, hardware utilization, and active database connections. It also features built-in query diagnostics and performance tracking for AlloyDB’s columnar engine, enabling quick troubleshooting of bottlenecks without manual terminal commands. To learn more about setting up this monitoring interface, read the fullAlloyDB Omni Web UI Blog Post.

    Semantic model routing replaces rigid static paths with a lightweight helper model to dynamically classify and dispatch intent-driven LLM traffic. Join Saravanakumar Rajagopal on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to leverage Antigravity and skills to architect these intelligent multi-provider routing patterns natively inside Apigee. Discover how to optimize your AI infrastructure and enhance flexibility at scale.

    Register for the November 12 Community TechTalk

Oct 19 - Oct 23

  • From prompt to production: End-to-end AI workflows in Apigee

    Deploying an enterprise AI gateway does not require deep API or machine learning expertise. Using declarative workflows in Apigee, teams can spin up a fully governed LLM gateway in minutes using a few environment variables. Join Luis Cuellar on Thursday, October 29, 2026 for a Community TechTalk exploring end-to-end AI workflows. Discover how to layer essential defenses—including Model Armor for prompt protection, Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) for sensitive data redaction, rate limiting, and response caching—before routing autonomous agent interactions through your gateway filters.

    Register for the October 29 Community TechTalk
  • Zero Standing Privileges with PAM: On-Demand Temporary Access for Humans and AI Agents

    AI agents now hand work off to other agents, risking stacked privileges and overpermissioning. Because agents plan their actions on the fly, permanent admin access means one hallucination can cascade into production. Join us on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 8:30 AM PST to see how Google CloudPrivileged Access Manager (PAM) brings Zero Standing Privileges to AI delegation, putting humans in command with cloud-native control that doesn't slow developers down.

    Register for the November 18 webinar
  • Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs

    Native streaming support is now in Public Preview for API Gateway, enabling you to run real-time and AI workloads behind your existing gateway. You can now route Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding without modifying your API spec or managing a split estate. This update also strengthens integration with the Gemini platform, allowing you to stream responses from Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI gpt-oss models seamlessly while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability.

    Read the blog to get started

Oct 12 - Oct 16

  • AI tokenomics in action: Enforcing tiered token budgets with Apigee

    Scaling artificial intelligence across an enterprise requires clear token governance to keep LLM spend predictable across departments. Join Tarun Abraham on Thursday, November 5, 2026 for a Community TechTalk on AI tokenomics. Discover how to use Apigee to enforce isolated, tiered token budgets and model access for each team—such as assigning Engineering a dedicated budget for Gemini Pro while covering mixed usage for Marketing—without changing application code. Attendees will also gain access to a sample codebase featuring a reusable Shared Flow.

    Register for the November 5 Community TechTalk

Sept 28 - Oct 2

  • Claude Sonnet 5.5 is now available on Google Cloud. Built for focused coding and knowledge work, it delivers stronger performance for feature development, and creating presentation-ready documents, while offering more intelligence with a lower cost per task for most work at faster speed.

    Deploy Sonnet 5.5 directly from Model Garden with Google Cloud’s enterprise security, scale, and governance built in. Try it now.

  • Mastering Storage Management with Storage Intelligence

    In our new blog, explore practical strategies to modernize storage operations using Storage Intelligence Advisor and enhanced Batch Operations. See how customers like Shipt and Palo Alto Networks are using these features to manage their estates at scale. Today, Storage Intelligence is used by 25 of the top 50 GCS customers. 2 in 3 customers have Storage Intelligence enabled for over 90% of their storage footprint.

    Explore best practices on our blog
  • Cut Gen AI costs by 70% with Apigee X dynamic routing

    Generative AI deployments face a harsh cost-performance trade-off: static model selection either wastes budget or compromises quality. Discover how to build an Intelligent AI Gateway using Apigee X to dynamically evaluate prompt complexity in real-time. This new blueprint automatically routes simple queries to lightweight models (like Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite) and complex reasoning tasks to advanced models (like Gemini 3.7 Flash), achieving over 70% cost savings without sacrificing output quality.

    Read the guide to optimize your Gen AI architecture
  • AI Agent Clinic launches new hands-on session on production agent evaluations

    A new episode of the AI Agent Clinic is now available showing organizations how to move past manual "vibe checks" to build robust, production-grade agent evaluations. In this hands-on session, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) take DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent, and build an end-to-end eval pipeline in under an hour. Learn how to standardize multi-turn traces across any framework using OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, pair LLM judges with deterministic checkers, and catch silent quality regressions before shipping.

    Watch here
  • Drive AI impact: Join Google's Agentic Data Cloud event on Nov 4

    Every enterprise plans to adopt agentic AI within two years, but data bottlenecks hold them back—AI accesses just 45% of enterprise data today (MIT, 2026). Google's Agentic Data Cloud provides the trustworthy foundation and real-time context AI needs.Join our product leaders November 4th to explore the latest innovations across databases, analytics, business intelligence, and storage, and get direct answers in our executive Q&A with Google Data Cloud VP & GM Andi Gutmans.

    Register today!

Sept 21 - Sept 25

  • Master MCP tool authorization and agent governance with Apigee

    While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solves interoperability for autonomous AI agents, chained actions like CRM edits or database queries quickly expose systems to unauthorized execution. Join our technical deep dive on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 5:00 PM CEST featuring Christophe from Google Cloud. Learn how positioning Apigee between MCP clients and enterprise backends enables fine-grained authorization (FGA), complete audit trails, and policy evaluation via emerging standards like OpenID AuthZEN.

    Language and accessibility note: This session will be hosted in French, but non-French speakers can follow along seamlessly by turning on Google Meet live translated captions to read in English, Spanish, German, Portuguese, or Italian.

    Register for the October 1 Community TechTalk
  • Apigee Trace Viewer Tutorial: Capturing & Analyzing Proxy Traces

    Streamlining API proxy debugging just got easier with a new tutorial by Apigee Customer Engineer Tyler Ayers. The guide covers end-to-end instructions for capturing debug traces in both Google Cloud Apigee X (or Hybrid) and the local Apigee Emulator, extracting trace JSON data via the web UI or automated REST APIs, and analyzing execution flows, variable mutations, and latency bottlenecks using the open source Apigee Trace Viewer.

    Read the Apigee Trace Viewer guide today.
  • Automate Apigee proxy testing locally

    Catching errors early saves time and money. A new tutorial by Apigee customer engineer Tyler Ayers shows how to use the Apigee Local Emulator for automated testing. Learn to run tests locally, integrate them into CI/CD pipelines, and deploy on Google Cloud Run for shared sandboxes. This approach provides instant feedback and zero cloud costs, helping teams speed up deployment cycles.

    Read the tutorial
  • Scale your enterprise multi-agent systems with Apigee

    Deploying multi-agent architectures in production introduces critical hurdles around security, operational control, and runtime expenses. Discover how Apigee API Hub provides a central discovery surface to eliminate agent sprawl across tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and enterprise APIs. Learn how to turn existing backend services into secure MCP tools using Agent Gateway guardrails, while applying semantic caching and intelligent model routing to keep compounding token costs predictable.

    Join Google Cloud in Chicago in Oct.15 for The AI Evolution.Reserve your seat for Chicago
  • Automate Apigee proxy testing with the Apigee Local Emulator

    Waiting on remote deployments to validate API proxy logic slows down release cycles and increases infrastructure overhead. Join Nigel Walters on Thursday, October 8, 2026, at 5:00 PM CEST for a Community TechTalk on shift-left testing for Apigee. Discover how to use the Apigee Local Emulator and apigee-emulator-service to run sub-second assertion suites on local machines, automate CI/CD checks in GitHub Actions, and deploy ephemeral preview sandboxes on Google Cloud Run.

    Register for the October 8 Community TechTalk
  • Now in Public Preview: AI-assisted EKS-to-GKE migrations with deterministic guardrails

    Migrating complex Kubernetes estates from AWS EKS to GKE is traditionally high-friction and error-prone. Now in Public Preview, GKE Agentic Migration is an open-source agent plugin that replaces ad-hoc LLM prompting with an AI-assisted migration workflow protected by deterministic guardrails.

    Running locally in your development harness, it indexes source IaC, maps cloud-specific primitives (such as Karpenter to Custom Compute Classes), and validates configurations offline—delivering reviewable pull requests and data-migration runbooks with zero live cluster mutations.

    Learn more in theannouncement blog and try the plugin on GitHub.
  • Claude Opus 5.5 is now available on Google Cloud. Built for everyday complex tasks, it delivers stronger agentic coding, research, and analysis while handling long-running work at a lower cost per token. Google Cloud continues to provide enterprise customers with broad model choice to build, deploy, and scale their AI agents securely.

    Try ithere.
  • Import Delta Lake tables with Dataflow Job Builder!

    Migrating to borderless Lakehouse just got a lot easier. You can now import Delta Lake tables stored in Cloud Storage usingDataflow Job Builder, a no-code/low-code interface for authoring Dataflow pipelines. Because Dataflow is a fully managed service, you are spared the overhead of provisioning and managing virtual machines. For step-by-step guidance, check out the documentation here.

Sept 14 - Sept 18

  • Storage Intelligence Advisor for Google Cloud Storage is now GA

    Google Cloud Storage customers can now manage cloud storage more effectively with Storage Intelligence Advisor, delivering curated metrics, automated anomaly detection, and actionable recommendations right out of the box, with zero setup required.

    Advisor baselines activity across your projects and automatically detects four key anomalies: surges in operations, unexpected rises in cross-region egress, and spikes in errors. Each finding includes deep drill-down visibility into the resources driving the change, alongside prescriptive steps to remediate issues before they impact performance or cost.

    Learn more to get started with Storage Intelligence Advisor.
  • Build private WebSockets from Apigee X to Cloud Run

    Real-time AI agents and streaming architectures often require persistent, bidirectional connections. A new implementation guide by Apigee Customer Engineer Joel Gauci demonstrates how to establish private southbound connectivity between Apigee X and Cloud Run. Using Private Service Connect (PSC) and a Regional Internal Application Load Balancer, teams can enforce API governance and security policies at the edge while keeping backend services completely isolated from the public internet.

    Explore the step-by-step guide and open-source code
  • Connecting Gemini Enterprise Agent Runtime to Apigee with Private Service Connect 

    Deploying autonomous AI agents often presents security, compliance, and cost challenges. A new reference guide details how to build an end-to-end, private architecture between Gemini Enterprise Agent Runtime and Apigee. This design helps protect internal backends and manage token quotas.

    Read the full community guide and deploy the code
  • Discover what’s new and next in Apigee

    As enterprise architectures adapt to generative AI and autonomous workflows, Apigee is expanding its proven platform capabilities to support modern AI gateway use cases alongside traditional API management. Join our session on Thursday, September 24, featuring Apigee Product Manager Geir Sjurseth. Get an inside look at recent product releases, explore architectural patterns for securing models and agents, and bring your questions for the live Q&A.

    Register for the September 24 Apigee product update
  • Managed Service for Apache Kafka supports clusters with public Internet access!

    WithManaged Kafka public clusters, you can now produce and consume messages from clients outside your VPC—including your local machine, for faster, frictionless testing. Public clusters unlock use cases like IoT devices, retail storefronts, and telco network towers. Enable public access on new or existing clusters via the Google Cloud console, gcloud CLI, or REST API. Spin up your first public cluster, or reach out to kafka-hotline@google.com with questions.
  • Stream data directly into Bigtable using Bigtable subscriptions, now in Preview!

    You can write Pub/Sub messages to a Bigtable table with zero ETL withBigtable subscriptions. No pipelines, no code, delivered by the serverless, zero-ops experience you already know with Pub/Sub. Power your AI workloads, from model telemetry to real-time context engineering, without the overhead of managing complicated ETL pipelines. Built to be dependable, with native support for dead-letter topics. Try the feature today!

Sept 7 - Sept 10

  • Why Your Voice Agent Needs Session Auditing

    Moving voice agents to production demands robust quality monitoring. This guide dives deep into the inner workings of the Agent Development Kit (ADK) responsible for audio session auditing. Learn how the ADK's
    save_live_blob
    feature intercepts, buffers, and stores raw audio chunks during active Gemini Live sessions. We explore building an automated post-processing pipeline to seamlessly stitch these fragments into cohesive, playable audio files. Discover how to leverage these vital audio audit trails to monitor real-world interactions, diagnose failures, and ensure enterprise-grade reliability. Read the full guide here.
  • AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM Orchestrator now Generally Available

    AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM orchestrator is now Generally Available. The AlloyDB Omni Red Hat RPM orchestrator offers a new way to manage PostgreSQL-compatible workloads on bare metal or VM platforms, combining the high performance of AlloyDB, access to generative AI features and Gemini models to build AI agents and applications, and full automation. The orchestrator simplifies cluster provisioning and lifecycle management by allowing you to define reference architecture specifications, customizable by adjusting instance parameters, node configurations, and networking options — discover all details in full blog post.

Aug 31 - Sept 4

  • Automate VM guest software lifecycle with VM Extension Manager, now GA

    Google Cloud VM Extension Manager is now generally available, eliminating the need for custom startup scripts to manage guest OS extensions across Compute Engine fleets. Define declarative, project-wide policies that enforce desired software states across all regions and zones. Benefit from continuous drift detection with automatic self-healing, multi-zone phased rollouts with automated rollbacks on failure, and centralized fleet health visibility integrated with Cloud Monitoring.

    ExploreVM Extension Manager documentation
  • Assess Apigee migrations without a target environment

    Planning a migration to Apigee X or Hybrid? You can now assess your legacy Apigee Edge SaaS or OPDK environment earlier in your planning cycle. Using the updated --skip-target-validation flag in the Apigee Migration Assessment Tool, teams can generate a full inventory and establish scope baselines before target infrastructure or IAM credentials are provisioned.

    Read the guide to learn more.

  • Claude Fable 5.1 is now available on Agent Platform. It brings performance improvements over Fable 5 across reasoning, full-lifecycle coding, multi-tool workflows, and knowledge work.

    Anthropic also announced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, a solution that gives customers the option to safely deploy Anthropic’s most capable models while storing their data in cloud infrastructure they control.

    We continue to offer enterprise customers options across frontier models to build, deploy, and scale securely on Google Cloud.

Aug 24 - Aug 28

  • Grok 4.6 is now available in Preview on Gemini Enterprise. xAI's most capable model, built for coding, agentic tasks, and knowledge work, Grok 4.6 joins Grok 4.3 and Grok 4.20 in Model Garden and becomes the flagship of the Grok family. It supports reasoning, function calling, and structured output for multi-step agentic workflows, and accepts text and image input.

    Get started today
  • Empowering autonomous agents with advanced security governance

    AI agents offer incredible productivity gains, but granting them access to read emails, query databases, and trigger APIs introduces critical new security risks. In fact, 79% of tech leaders cite security and governance as their biggest challenge to scaling AI. Traditional tools are no longer enough to handle automated threats like prompt injection and dynamic permissions. Discover how forward-thinking enterprises are using secure-by-default design, agent identity governance, and human-in-the-loop controls to deploy agents with confidence.

    Read more
  • Stateful processing is available in BigQuery continuous queries in Preview

    Stateful operations significantly expand what’s possible with BigQuery continuous queries. This feature allows users to leverage functions like JOINs, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals.
  • Try out our feature here and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com!
  • Synthetic data generator tool is available for Managed Service for Kafka

    You’ve launched your first Kafka cluster. Now what? The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Tryour quickstart today!
  • Dataflow pipeline updates are faster & more flexible

    Dataflow pipeline updates can now stop-and-replace pipelines, a major addition to the existing in-place-update feature. The new parallel pipeline option accelerates the migration between the old & new pipeline, resulting in reduced disruption to your business. You can also set a timeout on drains that prevents runaway costs for your pipeliness in the event of stuck processing. This feature is generally available. Try it here!

Aug 17 - Aug 21

  • Webinar: Agent Identity as the backbone for secure AI innovation

    An AI agent with a stolen API key looks identical to a legitimate one. As autonomous agents scale across enterprise systems, static credentials and legacy IAM policies can no longer keep up with machine-speed execution. Join Shaun Liu, Product Manager at Google Cloud, on August 27 at 1 PM ET to explore Google Cloud’s vision for unifying agent, human, and nonhuman identity into a workload-centric platform using verifiable cryptographic identities (SPIFFE, ID-JAG, OAuth).

    Register for the webinar now

Aug 10 - Aug 14

  • Diagnosing Apigee Hybrid Cassandra Read Latency for Peak Performance

    Diagnose real-time Cassandra read latency and resolve API key verification bottlenecks in Apigee Hybrid with this step-by-step troubleshooting guide. Learn how to deploy a debugging client and query performance tables to maintain sub-millisecond response times.

    Read the Apigee Hybrid Cassandra Troubleshooting Guide
  • Keep moving with agents! The All Things Agentic Hackathon is officially live.

    We're challenging builders to build next-generation agents that take on the busy work and handle the heavy lifting in the background using Gemini 3.5 and Google Cloud. Compete for your share of $190,000 in prizes, cash, and Google Cloud credits! Submissions are open from August 3, 2026, to August 31, 2026.

    Learn more and register. Sign up for GEAR to get exclusive updates and your badge. #AllThingsAgenticHackathon
  • Accelerate PostgreSQL migrations using Gemini in Database Migration Service

    Enterprise database migrations often stall during the "last mile" of translating legacy stored procedures, triggers, and custom functions from Oracle or SQL Server. Database Migration Service (DMS) now provides AI-assisted code conversion powered by Gemini in Databases. By combining deterministic compiler rules for 1:1 syntax with Gemini contextual synthesis for complex procedural blocks, DMS converts legacy code into native PostgreSQL and AlloyDB with full schema awareness and side-by-side validation.

    Read the full blog post to learn how to streamline your database code conversion.
  • Compute Flex CUDs now available for G2 and G4 GPU VMs

    Compute Flexible Committed Use Discounts (Flex CUDs) are now available for G2 (NVIDIA L4) and G4 (NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000) VMs. You can now lock in predictable savings while retaining the flexibility to adapt across VM families, migrate between regions, and combine general-purpose compute, GKE, Cloud Run, and G2 & G4 GPU VMs under a single spend commitment. Flex CUDs for G-series VMs let you lock in savings today while preserving the agility to upgrade to latest hardware without disruption!

    Explore VM instance pricing or learn more about Flex CUDs.

    With the release of GCSFS2026.8.0, organisations can now unlock maximum ROI from their AI/ML infrastructure by eliminating data starvation on GPUs in PyTorch ecosystem when they are using Frameworks like Dask, Pandas, PyTorch , PyTorch Lightning, Hugging Face Datasets, Ray dataetc. By making adaptive concurrent prefetching the default, GCSFS dynamically predicts and background-fetches sequential read patterns—boosting single-file throughput by 5x, and scaling up to 21 GiB/s , saturating the NIC when paired with Rapid Bucket. Aug 3 - Aug 7

Data from the 2026 State of AI Infrastructure report reveals that 52% of IT leaders are adopting hybrid cloud strategies to bridge this gap. Our latest blog post explores how Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) helps organizations deploy connected or air-gapped models to run advanced AI entirely within secure environments—mitigating geopolitical risks without sacrificing innovation.Read more.

    For years, enterprises have struggled with the cost, risk, and complexity of moving mission-critical SAP data into advanced analytics platforms. The general availability of SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) Connect for BigQuery marks a turning point. By introducing revolutionary zero-copy, bi-directional data sharing, this new capability seamlessly bridges SAP systems with Google Cloud's powerful data and AI ecosystem. Instead of wrestling with manual data duplication and lost business context, organizations can now eliminate silos, dramatically lower their analytics costs, and rapidly deploy trustworthy, agentic AI solutions grounded in real-time operational reality.Read the full announcement to learn how to transform your data strategy.

entries.title: Introducing Z4M: storage-optimized compute for AI/ML and parallel file systems
entries.summary: Today, we’re excited to announce the general availability of our next-generation Storage-optimized Z4M machine series in Google Compute Engine, available as both Virtual Machine (VM) and bare-metal instances. We built Z4M to provide storage for AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing, distributed key-value (KV) cache and parallel file systems — workloads that handle huge data
entries.content:
bob Napaa

Product Management

Today, we’re excited to announce the general availability of our next-generation Storage-optimized Z4M machine series in Google Compute Engine, available as both Virtual Machine (VM) and bare-metal instances. 

We built Z4M to provide storage for AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing, distributed key-value (KV) cache and parallel file systems — workloads that handle huge data volumes and require massive parallel data processing, as well as high storage and networking throughput. Low latency access to data is equally critical to keep GPUs and TPUs fully utilized. Powered by the fifth-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors and paired with the latest enhancements in Titanium, Z4M provides up to 168,000 GiB of Local SSD (LSSD) storage coupled with up to 400 Gbps of Cloud Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) networking. RDMA improves the performance of these demanding workloads by reducing data-access latency by up to 60% compared to TCP networking, so you can increase your applications’ throughput while right-sizing your cloud investment. 

Z4M VMs and bare-metal instances

The Z4M VM portfolio lets you scale your infrastructure and clusters to meet workload requirements by providing a large total LSSD capacity as well as 875 GiB of LSSD capacity per vCPU. Further, Z4M bare-metal instances give you direct access to the physical hardware without a virtualization layer, reducing latency for workloads such as custom hypervisors and workloads with specific licensing needs. Z4M bare-metal instances are also ideal for agentic AI workloads, enabling developers to run isolated sandboxes at scale, including with Agent Substrate.

In addition to 168,000 GiB of LSSD storage, Z4M VMs and bare metal instances offer up to 192 vCPUs and up to 1,536 GiB of memory for at-scale data processing. Z4M instances are based on Titanium SSDs, which offload local storage processing from CPU resources to deliver real-time data processing, low-latency, high-throughput storage performance and enhanced storage security. Z4M delivers up to 15.6M random-read IOPS and up to 75,600 MiB/s sequential-read throughput, improving the LSSD storage performance and throughput compared to Z3 by up to 70% and 110% respectively. 

Cloud RDMA and direct storage access

Z4M provides low-latency access to the storage layer using 400 Gbps of RDMA-enabled standard networking.This helps keep GPUs and TPUs fully utilized even when processing large multimodal datasets, by transferring massive amounts of data at line rate using NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage and TPUDirect Storage. At the same time, Z4M transfers data at full line rate while processing data locally, with a balanced-LSSD-to-networking-throughput ratio of 1.4:1. 

Built for demanding workloads

What customers and partners are saying

"Nutanix is committed to helping organizations run their applications and data anywhere. Bringing Nutanix Cloud Clusters (NC2) to Google Cloud's new Z4M metal instances reflects that mission and our continued partnership with Google Cloud. By combining Z4M’s exceptional I/O performance and high storage density along with Intel’s advanced compute and AMX-driven efficiency, NC2 on Z4M provides the scale, density, and performance required to power everything from dense VDI clusters to demanding, data-intensive AI workloads." - Saveen Pakala, Vice President of Product Management, Nutanix

"Google's Z4M VMs bring Cloud RDMA to a storage-optimized VM with much higher local SSD density than previous generations. In our testing, Cloud RDMA on Z4M demonstrated outstanding performance with up to 3.7x lower latency and up to 6x lower CPU usage than TCP. For our customers, that means faster, more predictable performance across a wide variety of use cases, from I/O-intensive databases to analytics and AI workloads, with the storage density to scale capacity efficiently." - Adik Sokolovski, Chief R&D Officer, Silk

“We're excited to support Google Cloud's new Z4M platform as part of the Sycomp Intelligent Data Storage Platform. With greater capacity per node and the continued evolution of the Z-series architecture, Z4M helps customers achieve new levels of performance and efficiency. Supporting innovations like Z4M reinforces Sycomp's commitment to delivering high-performance storage solutions across the Google Cloud ecosystem.” - Scott Fadden, Senior HPC Solutions Architect, Sycomp

"We've worked alongside Google Cloud for years on the most demanding AI and machine learning workloads. In our testing, we found the new Z4M machines deliver roughly twice the read throughput and up to 79% more IOPS, generation over generation (Z3 family). This means more data, more tokens, and more finished work. We’re excited to see what our joint customers build with these powerful machines." - Ajay Singh, Chief Product Officer, WEKA

Orchestration with Cluster Director

You can easily configure, deploy and manage large Z4M clusters using Google Cloud’s Cluster Director, which offers advanced placement and maintenance capabilities alongside the Cluster Toolkit for rapid cluster deployment. You can view and deploy your workloads in a compact topology to maximize performance, or spread topology for high availability by targeting availability domains. You can combine or stagger the maintenance across these availability domains. Additionally, you can co-locate Z4M instances with your GPU and TPU clusters to process very large datasets in real time and at scale. 

Enhanced maintenance experience

Both Z4M VMs and bare-metal instances make it easier for you to plan ahead and schedule maintenance operations by providing notice from the system several days in advance of required maintenance. For Z4M VMs with 42,000 GiB or less of LSSD storage, you can live-migrate an instance during maintenance events. Z4M VMs with 84,000 GiB or more of LSSD and Z4M bare metal instances must be terminated and restarted while preserving your data through planned maintenance events.

Support for Hyperdisk

Z4M VMs and bare-metal instances support Hyperdisk, Google Cloud’s workload-optimized block storage, which lets you optimize the performance for each workload by independently tuning the storage performance and capacity for each instance.

Specifically, they are compatible with Hyperdisk Balanced, Hyperdisk Throughput, and Extreme Hyperdisk storage for scalable, high-performance network-attached storage, supporting up to 512 TiB of capacity per instance. For general-purpose workloads, Hyperdisk Balanced, with up to 320K IOPS per instance, offers a mix of performance and cost-efficiency. Hyperdisk Extreme delivers ultra-low latency and supports up to 500K IOPS and 12,500 MiB/s throughput per Z4M VM and bare-metal instance, making it well-suited for demanding database workloads. 

Get started with Z4M today

Z4M VMs and bare metal instances are available today in select regions worldwide. To start using Z4M instances, choose Z4M under the Storage-Optimized machine family when creating a new VM or GKE node pool in the Google Cloud console. Learn more at the Z4M machine series page. Contact your Google Cloud sales representative for more information on regional availability.
